planting.note: Plant container-grown stock or rooted cuttings in spring, since seed viability is short-lived and germination is slow and erratic; set out after soil has warmed and frost risk has passed.

directions: Mexican bay is a small aromatic tree or large shrub in the laurel family, native to pine-oak and cloud forests at mid-to-high elevations across Mexico and Central America, where the dried leaves are sold in markets as 'laurel' and used exactly like Mediterranean bay leaf to season beans, soups, and stews. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil with partial shade, especially in hotter climates, and allow several years for the tree to reach a harvestable size. Because wild populations have been heavily overharvested for the leaf trade and the species is now listed as endangered in parts of its native range, cultivated garden or nursery stock is preferable to wild-collected leaf. Harvest mature leaves selectively and dry them in a shaded, well-ventilated spot before storing airtight.

planting.note: Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings and set out rooted plants in spring, since seed set is sparse and unreliable in cultivation.

directions: Oreganillo is a woody-based aromatic shrub native to temperate pine-oak highlands across central and southern Mexico, from Jalisco and Michoacan east through the states of Mexico, Morelos, Guerrero, Puebla, and Oaxaca, where its camphor-mint-anise-scented leaves are used fresh or dried both as a cooking seasoning and brewed as a traditional herbal tea valued in folk use for digestion. Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly gravelly soil in full sun and avoid overwatering, since the species comes from dry, rocky mountain slopes. Harvest leafy stem tips just before flowering for the strongest aroma, and prune after flowering to keep the shrub compact and encourage fresh new growth. In colder zones grow it in a container and bring it under cover when temperatures drop much below freezing.

planting.note: Start indoors well ahead of last frost, since Eryngium seed germinates slowly and erratically; transplant out once seedlings are well rooted and frost risk has passed.

directions: Hierba del sapo is a spiny-leaved, thistle-like rosette-forming perennial native to the high volcanic grasslands and oak woodlands of central Mexico, where the leaves and roots are traditionally infused into pulque to make the well-known curado de hierba del sapo and used as a folk digestive remedy. Sow in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun and expect slow, uneven germination typical of the genus. Once established, the rosettes tolerate drought, poor soil, and light frost with little care. Harvest outer leaves selectively, leaving the central rosette intact so the plant continues producing new growth.
sources: Mexican traditional pulque and herbal-medicine literature
